modules.title: Core Java & OOP
modules.intro: Core Java interview questions are the foundation of every Java backend interview. This page covers the language fundamentals interviewers actually probe — exception handling (checked vs unchecked, try-with-resources), generics and type erasure, reflection, the Java I/O and NIO APIs, string immutability, and the small comparisons that recur in every loop (== vs equals, Comparable vs Comparator, abstract class vs interface). For pure object-oriented design questions (encapsulation, polymorphism, SOLID applied to Java) head to the dedicated Java OOP page. Each answer is structured the way you would actually answer in a 45-minute interview: the headline, the why, a code-shaped example, and the trade-off the interviewer is really listening for.

modules.title: Java OOP & SOLID
modules.intro: Java OOP interview questions are the single most common opener in any backend interview, from junior to staff. This page is dedicated to object-oriented design in Java — the four pillars (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction), access modifiers, abstract classes vs interfaces, composition vs inheritance, and the SOLID principles applied to real Java code. Expect questions that test conceptual depth ("explain Liskov substitution with an example") as well as design judgement ("would you use an abstract class or an interface here, and why?"). Every answer comes with a short code snippet, the trade-off the interviewer is listening for, and the follow-up they are likely to ask next.

modules.title: Java Collections & Algorithms
modules.intro: Java Collections interview questions test how well you understand the framework you reach for every day — ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap internals, the contract between equals() and hashCode(), iteration safety, and which Set/Queue to pick under contention. This page covers the framework alongside the algorithm questions interviewers pair with it (Big-O for common operations, sorting, searching, sliding window, two pointers, tree and graph traversal, basic DP). For thread-safe collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) and the concurrency primitives behind them, see the Java Concurrency page. Each answer leads with the structural insight ("a HashMap is an array of buckets...") then drops into the implementation details senior interviewers actually probe.

modules.title: Java Streams, Lambdas & Modern Java
modules.intro: Java Streams, Lambdas and Modern Java interview questions cover what you need to write idiomatic post-Java-8 code: lambdas and functional interfaces, the Streams API (map/filter/reduce/collect, intermediate vs terminal, lazy evaluation), Optional, and the language features added between Java 9 and 21 (the module system, records, sealed classes, pattern matching, virtual threads, structured concurrency). Interviewers often test whether you actually understand the cost model — when streams help versus when a simple loop is faster — and whether you can spot the bug in a parallel stream. Each answer is structured around the interview-grade insight, not the API reference.

modules.title: Java Concurrency & Multithreading
modules.intro: Java Concurrency and Multithreading interview questions are where senior interviews are won or lost. This page covers threads and the Thread lifecycle, the Java Memory Model (happens-before, volatile vs synchronized), synchronization and locks, the ExecutorService and thread pools, CompletableFuture, concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap internals), virtual threads (Java 21+ Project Loom), and the patterns interviewers actually ask about (producer-consumer, CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore). Every answer leads with the conceptual model, then the API, then the failure mode that distinguishes a 3-year engineer from a 10-year one.

modules.title: JVM Internals & Performance
modules.intro: JVM internals interview questions show up in every senior Java backend interview — class loading, the runtime memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace), garbage collection (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, when to pick which), JIT compilation, escape analysis, and the diagnostic tools you reach for in a production incident (jstack, jmap, async-profiler, JFR). This page covers the questions that test depth: "walk me through what happens between System.out.println and the bytes hitting the kernel", "why is this app's tail latency so bad", "how would you tune the GC for a high-throughput service". Each answer is structured for an interview, not a textbook — concept first, then the trade-offs.

modules.title: Spring Core & IoC
modules.intro: Spring Core interview questions test whether you understand the framework underneath Spring Boot — the IoC container, dependency injection (constructor vs setter vs field), bean lifecycles and scopes, the BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext, AOP fundamentals (proxies, advices, pointcuts), and the @Transactional internals interviewers love to probe. This page covers the conceptual layer that lets you debug a real Spring app instead of just write one. Pair this page with the Spring Boot page (auto-configuration, starters, profiles), Spring Data JPA / Hibernate, Spring Security, Spring WebFlux, and Spring Batch.

modules.title: Spring Boot
modules.intro: Spring Boot interview questions are the single most asked Spring topic — auto-configuration internals, the starter system, application.properties/yml + profiles, Actuator endpoints and security, embedded servers, configuration binding, graceful shutdown, scheduled tasks, layered Docker images, and the troubleshooting questions interviewers pull from real production incidents. This page covers the questions that test whether you have actually shipped Spring Boot to production, not just used start.spring.io. For lower-level Spring concepts (IoC, AOP, transaction internals) see Spring Core; for persistence see Spring Data JPA / Hibernate.

modules.title: Spring Data, JPA & Hibernate
modules.intro: Hibernate and JPA interview questions are a staple of every Java backend interview — the entity lifecycle, persistence context and the first-level cache, lazy vs eager fetching, the dreaded N+1 query problem and its solutions (entity graphs, JOIN FETCH, projections), @Transactional propagation, optimistic vs pessimistic locking, second-level cache, batching, and the differences between JPA, Hibernate, MyBatis and JOOQ. This page covers every Hibernate/JPA question that recurs in interviews, with code snippets and the SQL Hibernate actually emits. Expect senior interviews to dig into transaction internals and connection-pool sizing — both covered here in depth.

modules.title: Spring Security & Identity
modules.intro: Spring Security interview questions cover the auth layer that protects every modern Java backend — the SecurityFilterChain, authentication providers, password encoding, session vs stateless (JWT) auth, OAuth2 and OpenID Connect, method-level security (@PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize), CORS and CSRF, and the common pitfalls interviewers love to surface (storing JWTs in localStorage, missing audit fields, leaking principal in logs). This page covers Spring Security with Spring Boot 3, including the modern config-by-bean style and the migration patterns from the older WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter approach.

modules.title: Spring WebFlux & Reactive Programming
modules.intro: Spring WebFlux interview questions test whether you understand reactive programming on the JVM — Mono vs Flux, backpressure, the Project Reactor operator vocabulary, Schedulers and threading, when reactive helps versus when it just adds complexity, and the migration patterns from blocking Spring MVC. This page is small but focused: each question is one a senior interviewer actually asks when WebFlux is on your resume.

modules.title: Spring Batch & Scheduling
modules.intro: Spring Batch interview questions cover the batch-processing framework that powers reconciliation, ETL and reporting jobs in every regulated Java backend — the Job/Step/Tasklet/Chunk model, ItemReader/Processor/Writer, restart and skip logic, partitioning and parallel steps, JobRepository internals, and the integration patterns that show up in finance and telco interviews. Each answer leads with the framework concept, then the operational concern interviewers really want to hear.

modules.title: SQL & Relational Databases
modules.intro: SQL interview questions are unavoidable in any backend interview — joins (inner, outer, cross, self), subqueries vs joins, window functions, indexes (B-tree vs hash, when an index hurts), the EXPLAIN plan, transaction isolation levels, ACID, normalization, sharding, partitioning, replication, connection pooling, and migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase). This page covers cross-database SQL fundamentals plus the operational questions that decide a senior interview. For Postgres-specific deep dives (window functions, JSONB, MVCC, partitioning), use the dedicated PostgreSQL page; for MongoDB, see the MongoDB page; for Redis, see the Redis page.

modules.title: PostgreSQL
modules.intro: PostgreSQL interview questions go beyond generic SQL — MVCC and the PostgreSQL transaction model, JSONB indexing strategies, partitioning (declarative + inheritance), the rich window-function vocabulary, replication (streaming + logical), backup and PITR strategy, query planning with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and the Spring Boot + HikariCP tuning patterns that surface in real interviews. This page is the one to use when the job description specifies Postgres (which is most of them in 2026).

modules.title: NoSQL & MongoDB
modules.intro: MongoDB interview questions cover the document data model in interview depth — schema design (embedded vs referenced), indexes (compound, multikey, text, geo), the aggregation pipeline, sharding and zone sharding, replica sets and read concerns, consistency trade-offs (eventual, causal, linearizable reads), and integration with Spring Data MongoDB. Expect senior interviews to compare MongoDB to a relational store and probe on operational concerns (rebalancing, backup, election).

modules.title: Redis & Caching
modules.intro: Redis and caching interview questions test whether you understand caching as a system, not just a library — Redis data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, HyperLogLog), eviction policies (LRU, LFU, allkeys vs volatile), persistence (RDB, AOF), replication and Sentinel/Cluster modes, cache-aside vs read-through vs write-back, distributed locking (Redlock and its critics), and the common pitfalls (cache stampede, hot keys, big keys). This page is the one to use for any role that mentions Redis or distributed caching.

modules.title: REST API & Spring MVC
modules.intro: REST API interview questions are core to every Java backend role — RESTful constraints, HTTP semantics and status codes, idempotency, request/response design, error handling, validation, pagination (cursor vs offset), HATEOAS, API versioning, OpenAPI/Swagger, HTTP clients (RestTemplate, WebClient, Feign), HTTP caching (ETag, Cache-Control), and Spring MVC controller fundamentals. For GraphQL-specific questions see the dedicated GraphQL page; for gRPC see the gRPC page.

modules.title: GraphQL with Spring
modules.intro: GraphQL interview questions test whether you understand the query-language alternative to REST — schema design (types, queries, mutations, subscriptions), resolvers, the N+1 problem and DataLoader, schema federation, persisted queries, error handling, security (depth limiting, query cost analysis), and the integration patterns with Spring for GraphQL. Expect the interviewer to compare GraphQL to REST and ask when you would choose each — that question is covered in depth here.

modules.title: gRPC for Java Services
modules.intro: gRPC interview questions cover the high-performance RPC framework increasingly common in microservice interviews — Protocol Buffers (proto3), the four service types (unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidi), interceptors, deadlines and cancellation, load balancing, gRPC vs REST vs messaging trade-offs, and the gRPC + Spring Boot integration patterns. This page is the one to use for any role that mentions internal service-to-service RPC at scale.

modules.title: Microservices Architecture
modules.intro: Microservices interview questions test architectural judgement, not just framework knowledge — service decomposition, API gateway patterns, service discovery, client- vs server-side load balancing, circuit breaker / retry / bulkhead / time limiter (Resilience4j), saga and outbox patterns, distributed tracing (correlation IDs, OpenTelemetry, Zipkin), config management (Spring Cloud Config), service mesh (sidecars, Istio basics), and the migration patterns from monolith to microservices (strangler fig). Pair this with the REST API and Messaging/Kafka pages for the full microservices interview surface.

modules.title: Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture
modules.intro: Kafka and event-driven architecture interview questions cover the messaging system that powers most modern Java backends — Kafka architecture (brokers, topics, partitions, consumer groups, ISR), delivery semantics (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), idempotent consumers, the outbox pattern, schema evolution, Kafka Streams vs Flink vs Spark Streaming, the saga pattern with choreography, CQRS and event sourcing, and Spring Kafka / Spring Cloud Stream. For RabbitMQ-specific questions (exchange types, routing, DLX), see the dedicated RabbitMQ page.

modules.title: RabbitMQ & AMQP
modules.intro: RabbitMQ interview questions cover the AMQP-based broker still common in finance, telco and any Java backend that needs flexible routing — exchange types (direct, fanout, topic, headers), bindings and routing keys, queue durability and message persistence, dead-letter exchanges and DLQ patterns, prefetch and consumer ack strategies, publisher confirms, clustering and quorum queues, and the Spring AMQP integration patterns. Use this page when the role specifies RabbitMQ over Kafka.

modules.title: Design Patterns & SOLID
modules.intro: Design patterns interview questions test whether you can apply the Gang-of-Four classics to real Java code — Singleton (and why it is a smell), Factory and Abstract Factory, Builder (with the Java records angle), Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter, Proxy, and the patterns Spring itself uses (Template Method, IoC, AOP). Each answer leads with the problem the pattern solves, the Java implementation, and the trade-offs (when not to use it).

modules.title: Architecture Patterns & Principles
modules.intro: Software architecture interview questions cover the higher-level patterns senior interviews probe — layered vs hexagonal vs clean architecture, DDD (entities, aggregates, bounded contexts, ubiquitous language), CQRS and event sourcing, the SOLID principles applied at the system level, modular monolith vs microservices, and the architectural trade-offs interviewers love to discuss (consistency vs availability, cohesion vs coupling). Use this page for staff/principal-level interviews where the question is rarely "how would you implement X" and more often "how would you decompose Y".

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.intro: System design interview questions are the differentiator for senior and staff Java backend roles — capacity estimation, the building blocks (load balancers, caches, queues, databases, CDNs), data partitioning, replication and consistency, rate limiting, idempotency at scale, designing for high availability, and the trade-offs that show up in every system-design round (latency vs throughput, consistency vs availability). This page covers the fundamentals; for full case studies (URL shortener, Twitter feed, distributed cache) see the System Design Problems page.

modules.title: System Design Case Studies
modules.intro: System design problem walkthroughs — full end-to-end designs for the cases interviewers actually ask: URL shortener, distributed cache, rate limiter, news feed, ride-sharing dispatch, payment system, notification service, real-time chat. Each case follows the same structure: requirements, capacity estimation, API design, data model, high-level architecture, deep dives into the bottleneck components, and the trade-offs you would articulate to the interviewer. Pair this with the System Design Fundamentals page.

modules.title: Application Security & OWASP
modules.intro: Application security interview questions cover the OWASP top issues every senior backend engineer is expected to know — injection (SQL, command), broken authentication and session management, XSS and CSRF, insecure deserialization, dependency vulnerabilities (CVE triage, Log4Shell-grade incidents), secrets management, secure password storage (bcrypt/argon2), TLS basics, and the secure-by-default patterns in modern Spring Boot. Pair this with the Spring Security page for the auth-specific surface.

modules.title: Java Testing
modules.intro: Java testing interview questions cover the full testing pyramid — unit testing with JUnit 5 (lifecycle, parameterized tests, extensions), mocking with Mockito (verify, argument matchers, when not to mock), Spring Boot test slices, integration testing with Testcontainers, contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract), TDD discipline, performance testing, chaos testing, and the trade-offs between mocks vs real dependencies. This page covers JUnit, Mockito, Testcontainers and the testing-strategy questions that come up at every level.

modules.title: Git
modules.intro: Git interview questions cover the version control system every developer touches daily — the difference between merge and rebase (and when to use each), interactive rebase for cleaning history, git bisect for finding the commit that broke a test, cherry-pick vs merge for backporting, resolving merge conflicts, Git hooks for code quality, monorepo vs polyrepo trade-offs, GitFlow vs trunk-based development, and the production scenarios interviewers love ("someone committed a secret to git — what now?"). For Maven/Gradle build-tool questions, see the Java Build Tools page.

modules.title: Maven & Gradle (Java Build Tools)
modules.intro: Java build tool interview questions cover Maven and Gradle in interview depth — Maven lifecycle phases, dependency scopes and conflict resolution, multi-module projects, profiles, publishing artifacts; Gradle build scripts, the dependency DSL, the wrapper, multi-module builds, incremental builds, and the Maven-vs-Gradle decision (and Bazel as the third option). Use this page for any role that touches CI builds, library publishing, or migrating between build tools.

modules.title: CI/CD Pipelines
modules.intro: CI/CD interview questions cover the pipelines that ship every modern Java backend — GitHub Actions vs Jenkins vs GitLab CI, declarative Jenkins pipelines, secret management, deployment strategies (blue/green, canary, rolling, feature flags), trunk-based development, automated rollback on SLO regression, and the production debugging questions interviewers love ("the pipeline is suddenly 4x slower — what now?"). For Terraform/IaC questions, see the dedicated Terraform page; for Jenkins-specific deep dives, see the Jenkins page.

modules.title: Terraform & Infrastructure-as-Code
modules.intro: Terraform and Infrastructure-as-Code interview questions cover the tool that provisions most modern cloud infrastructure — providers, resources, state management (and remote state), modules, workspaces, the plan/apply lifecycle, drift detection, secrets handling, and the patterns for multi-environment deployments. Use this page for any DevOps/SRE role where IaC ownership is part of the job spec.

modules.title: Jenkins CI
modules.intro: Jenkins interview questions cover the CI server still running half the world's Java backend pipelines — declarative vs scripted pipelines, Jenkinsfile structure, agents, shared libraries, credentials and secrets, plugin ecosystem, multi-branch pipelines, and the upgrade-and-stability concerns that come up in interviews for Jenkins-heavy shops. For broader CI/CD comparisons (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI), see the CI/CD page.

modules.title: Docker & Containerization
modules.intro: Docker interview questions cover the container runtime every backend engineer is expected to know — image layers and caching, Dockerfile best practices, multi-stage builds, the difference between ENTRYPOINT and CMD, networking modes, volumes and bind mounts, image security (non-root, distroless), and the Spring Boot-specific patterns (layered jars, jib). For orchestration, see the Kubernetes page.

modules.title: Kubernetes & Orchestration
modules.intro: Kubernetes interview questions are now standard for any senior Java backend role — pods, deployments, services, ingress, ConfigMaps and Secrets, HPA and resource requests/limits, StatefulSets and persistent volumes, rolling updates and rollback, network policies, RBAC, and the production-debugging questions interviewers ask ("a pod is in CrashLoopBackOff — walk me through your debug"). Pair this page with the Docker, CI/CD and Cloud-Native pages for the full container-platform interview surface.

modules.title: AWS, Cloud & Cloud-Native Architecture
modules.intro: AWS interview questions are unavoidable in any cloud-leaning backend interview — the core compute services (EC2 vs ECS vs EKS vs Fargate vs Lambda), RDS and Aurora and DynamoDB, S3 and storage classes, IAM (roles vs users, least privilege, the trust policy that always confuses), the messaging stack (SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis), serverless patterns with Lambda + Spring Cloud Function, and the production-debug scenarios interviewers actually ask ("the AWS bill doubled overnight — debug it"). For vendor-agnostic cloud-native patterns (12-factor, deployment strategies, DR) see the Cloud Native page; for GCP and Azure see the dedicated platform pages.

modules.title: Cloud-Native & Cloud Architecture
modules.intro: Cloud-native interview questions cover the cloud-vendor-agnostic patterns every modern backend interview probes — the 12-factor methodology, cloud design patterns (circuit breaker, bulkhead, retry-with-backoff, ambassador, sidecar), deployment strategies (rolling, blue/green, canary, progressive delivery), disaster recovery (RPO/RTO), multi-region active/active vs active/passive trade-offs, cost optimization (FinOps), and the orchestrator-choice question (Kubernetes vs ECS vs Cloud Run vs Lambda). Pair this with the AWS, GCP, Azure or Kubernetes pages for the platform-specific surface.

modules.title: Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
modules.intro: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) interview questions cover the platform powering an increasing share of Java backend roles — the core GCP services for backend developers (Cloud Run, GKE, Cloud SQL, Spanner, BigQuery), Pub/Sub messaging, Cloud Storage, IAM and Workload Identity, Secret Manager, Cloud Monitoring, and the deployment patterns for Spring Boot on Cloud Run vs GKE. Use this page when the job description specifies GCP — the questions are different enough from AWS that a generic cloud answer will not cut it.

modules.title: Microsoft Azure
modules.intro: Microsoft Azure interview questions cover the platform common in enterprise Java backend roles — Azure Spring Apps for managed Spring Boot, AKS and Azure Container Registry, Azure Functions for serverless Java, the storage stack (Blob, SQL Database, Cosmos DB), the messaging stack (Service Bus vs Event Hubs), Key Vault and Managed Identity for passwordless auth, Azure Active Directory with Spring Security, and Application Insights for observability. Use this page when the job description mentions Azure or Microsoft-shop tooling.

modules.title: Observability & Monitoring
modules.intro: Observability interview questions cover the three pillars (metrics, logs, traces) plus the engineering culture around them — Micrometer + Prometheus + Grafana, structured logging (JSON, MDC, correlation IDs), distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Zipkin, Jaeger), SLI/SLO/SLA definitions, error budgets, the four golden signals, alerting design (avoiding alert fatigue), and the pragmatic question every senior interview asks: "what would you instrument first in a brand-new service?". For incident response and on-call see the SRE page.

modules.title: Production Operations & SRE
modules.intro: SRE and production-operations interview questions cover the role that owns reliability for every modern Java backend — incident response and runbooks, postmortems and the blameless culture, on-call rotation design, error budgets and SLO-driven engineering, capacity planning, chaos engineering, the production-debug toolkit (jstack, jmap, async-profiler, JFR, eBPF), and the questions interviewers ask to test calm under pressure ("P0 fires — walk me through the first 15 minutes"). Pair this with the Observability page for the full production-engineering surface.

modules.title: Behavioral, Leadership & Engineering Practices
modules.intro: Behavioral interview questions are now equal-weighted with technical questions in every senior+ interview. This page covers the STAR method applied correctly, conflict resolution, agile/scrum scenarios, delivering under pressure, the failure-and-learning question (rehearsed but never canned), and career-growth narratives that do not sound rehearsed. For engineering-practice questions (code review, ADRs, technical debt, mentoring, technical leadership) see the Engineering Practices page — those are a separate, well-defined interview category.

modules.title: Engineering Practices & Technical Leadership
modules.intro: Engineering practices interview questions test whether you operate as a senior engineer outside the IDE — running effective code reviews, writing Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), managing technical debt strategically, building knowledge-sharing culture, mentoring junior engineers, leading cross-team initiatives, and the technical-leadership questions that come up at staff and principal level ("how would you approach the first 90 days on a team with high tech debt?"). Pair this with the Behavioral page for the full senior-interview narrative surface.

modules.title: Low-Level Design (LLD)
modules.intro: Low-level design (LLD) interview questions test whether you can take an ambiguous prompt ("design a parking lot", "design a cab-booking system") and produce a clean class diagram in 30 minutes — using OOP correctly, identifying entities and relationships, applying the right design patterns, and writing code that compiles. This page covers the LLD prompts that recur most often, with the classes, the patterns used, and the Java code skeletons.
